Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. - Q2 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. Q2 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Machinery Corp.'s results for the Q2 FY2024. Joining me on today's call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; and Michael Rivera, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Machinery Corp.'s performance for the Q2 FY2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, our aftermarket parts and services business delivered exceptional growth, reaching double-digit increases for the 11th straight quarter and now comprising a larger share of total revenue, bolstering our high-margin recurring streams amid robust fleet utilization in mining and construction. Second, revenue performance across geographic regions showed strength, with North America leading on reshoring trends, Asia-Pacific accelerating on infrastructure and EV demand, and balanced contributions from Europe and the rest of the world. Third, we've achieved meaningful reductions in lead times for our core products like CNC machining centers and hydraulic presses, down over 20% quarter-over-quarter through supply chain diversification and digital tools, enhancing our competitiveness. Finally, we're issuing positive revenue guidance for Q3 and the full year, reflecting solid backlog conversion and end-market tailwinds in automation and electrification.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Rivera to provide more detail on our financial results.

Michael Rivera (CFO):
Thank you, Johnathan. Turning to our financial performance, Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. reported $1.28 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year on a reported basis and 14% organically, excluding a 2% foreign exchange headwind. Gross margin was 32.1%, driven by pricing discipline, a favorable aftermarket mix, and operational efficiencies in our global service network. Operating expenses were $285 million, resulting in an operating income of $195 million. Our net income for the quarter was $140 million, or $1.85 per share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

As we dive deeper into the segment results, I'd like to spend some time on our aftermarket parts and services business, which continues to be the crown jewel of our portfolio. This high-margin, recurring revenue stream not only drives profitability but also builds sticky customer relationships in our core markets of heavy earthmoving equipment, CNC machining centers, and hydraulic systems for mining and construction applications.

In Q2, aftermarket parts and services revenue reached $458 million, up 14.2% year-over-year and 18% on an organic constant-currency basis. This marks our 11th straight quarter of double-digit growth, outpacing our new equipment sales by over 500 basis points. As a result, aftermarket now represents 37% of our total company revenue—up from 32% a year ago and well ahead of the industry average of around 25% for peers like Caterpillar and Komatsu. For context, our full-year 2023 aftermarket contribution was 34%, and we're on track to hit 38-40% for FY2024, assuming stable utilization rates.

Let me break down the key drivers of this growth. First, volume expansion from higher equipment utilization. Global fleet utilization for our installed base—primarily Cat 793-class haul trucks, our ApexForge CNC mills, and H-series hydraulic excavators—averaged 82% in Q2, up from 76% last year. This reflects the post-pandemic industrial rebound, with mining capex up 12% globally per Wood Mackenzie data, and U.S. non-residential construction starts holding steady at elevated levels despite high interest rates. Our parts content per machine, which we track rigorously, rose 9% YoY to $2,450 annualized, fueled by increased demand for wear items like bucket teeth, undercarriage components, and high-pressure hydraulic seals.

Second, pricing discipline added 4.5 points to growth. Average selling prices for genuine AIMC parts increased 5.2%, in line with steel and alloy input cost inflation of 3-4%, while services ASPs rose 6.8% due to labor premiumization. We've maintained book-to-bill ratios above 1.15x, ensuring we're not flooding the channel and protecting margins.

Third, services mix shift is accelerating. Remanufactured components—think our Reman Prime program for engine blocks and transmissions—grew 22% YoY to $112 million, capturing 25% of parts revenue. Full-service maintenance contracts, including our AIMC UptimeGuard predictive analytics platform, surged 28% to $89 million, now 19% of the segment. This is huge for recurring revenue stability; contract backlog stands at $2.1 billion, up 16% YoY, with a weighted average duration of 42 months.

On the technical front, our digital initiatives are paying off handsomely. We've now equipped over 65% of our active fleet—roughly 28,000 machines—with IoT sensors via the UptimeGuard ecosystem, similar to Caterpillar's Vital Metrics or Cummins' Connected Diagnostics. This enables predictive maintenance, reducing unplanned downtime by 22% for enrolled customers and driving a 35% uptick in service pulls. In Q2, AI-driven anomaly detection flagged 14,000 potential failures, averting $45 million in customer lost productivity. We're also rolling out digital twins for our ApexPress hydraulic presses, allowing virtual prototyping of upgrades that boost throughput by 15-20%. These tools have expanded our total addressable aftermarket from $18 billion to $22 billion, per internal modeling.

Regionally, performance was robust across the board. North America, 48% of segment revenue, grew 16% YoY, led by oil sands and copper mining ramps in Canada and Arizona. U.S. data center construction is pulling through demand for our precision CNC parts. Asia-Pacific, at 32%, delivered 20% growth—China infrastructure stimulus and Indian mining capex offsetting softer OEM volumes. EMEA, 15%, saw 9% growth despite automotive slowdowns, buoyed by wind turbine maintenance for our hydraulic yaw systems. Latin America rounded out at 5%, up 12% on Brazilian ag equipment rebuilds.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on margin expansion and customer lock-in. Segment-adjusted EBITDA margins hit 48.2% in Q2—up 210 bps YoY and 2,800 bps above new equipment—thanks to 65% gross margins on parts and scale in our 240 global service centers. We've invested $120 million YTD in dealer network densification, adding 35 locations in high-growth areas like Indonesia and Mexico, mirroring Ingersoll Rand's playbook. Partnerships with OEMs like Volvo CE for co-branded reman programs are opening white-space opportunities. Looking ahead, we're guiding Q3 aftermarket growth of 12-15% YoY, with FY2024 at 13-16%, implying $1.85-1.95 billion. Risks include potential softening in China real estate, but our diversified fleet and digital moat position us well.

In summary, aftermarket isn't just growing—it's transforming AIMC into a services-led industrial powerhouse, much like GE's pivot years ago. This segment's resilience underscores our 'Equipment + Intelligence' strategy, delivering superior ROIC of 28% versus 14% for new sales.

Before moving on, let me set the context on our overall revenue breakdown by geographic region, which we report based on customer shipment destination. Our diversification across regions continues to be a key strength, mitigating macro volatility. This marks our sixth straight quarter of double-digit organic growth, driven by robust demand for our next-gen automation platforms amid the global push toward Industry 4.0 and supply chain reshoring. Bookings were $1.35 billion, up 15% YoY, with backlog now at a record $4.2 billion, providing strong visibility into H2 and FY25.

North America, 45% of Q2 revenue at $576 million, grew 18% YoY organically. It remains our largest and highest-margin region, fueled by unprecedented reshoring and nearshoring trends. U.S. revenue grew 20% organically to $510 million, with Canada adding another 8%. Key drivers included a surge in semiconductor fab equipment orders—our high-precision CNC lathes and robotic wafer handlers saw 25% YoY uptake from clients like Intel and TSMC's new Arizona plants. Automotive OEMs, including Ford and GM, ramped capex for EV battery assembly lines, boosting demand for our modular stamping presses. Aerospace also shone, with Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems pulling forward deliveries of our titanium-machining centers amid supply chain normalization. Strategically, we're investing $150 million in our Dayton, Ohio, facility to expand capacity for AI-integrated robotics, targeting a 20% ASP uplift from software-as-a-service bundles. Margins here expanded 220 basis points to 28%, thanks to localized sourcing and reduced ocean freight costs versus Asia.

Europe, 28% of Q2 revenue at $358 million, grew 9% YoY organically after adjusting for a 3% FX drag from the weakening euro. Germany led at +12% ($140 million), driven by our Fanuc-compatible robotic arms for battery gigafactories—Volkswagen and Northvolt accounted for 15% of regional bookings. The UK grew 10% on energy transition plays, with our gas turbine maintenance equipment gaining traction at Siemens Energy sites. However, we saw softness in Italy and France (-2% combined) due to lingering industrial slowdowns and high energy costs post-Ukraine crisis. Initiatives like our 'EuroGreen' sustainability certification for low-emission presses helped win ESG-focused tenders, and we're eyeing a JV with a Danish wind OEM to penetrate renewables. Regional margins held steady at 24%, but we expect 50 bps expansion in H2 from pricing actions and supply chain efficiencies.

Asia-Pacific, 20% of Q2 revenue at $256 million, grew 16% YoY organically, our fastest-growing region. China was +14% ($120 million) despite uneven recovery—strong semi demand from SMIC and Huawei offset softer consumer electronics. India exploded +35% to $45 million, propelled by our partnerships with Tata Motors for EV stamping lines and Reliance for smart factory retrofits. Southeast Asia, including Vietnam and Thailand, grew 22% on electronics reshoring, where our IoT edge-computing modules for assembly lines mirrored success seen at Foxconn facilities. Japan and Korea were flat at +2%, cyclical in autos but buoyed by memory chip expansions at Samsung. We're doubling down with a $200 million greenfield plant in Chennai, India, to localize 70% of APAC production by FY26, reducing lead times by 30% and countering U.S.-China trade tensions. Margins compressed slightly to 22% from mix shift toward lower-ASP emerging market volumes, but ASPs rose 8% on premium automation suites.

Rest of World, 7% of Q2 revenue at $90 million, grew 5% YoY organically. Latin America was up 12% ($40 million) on mining equipment for Brazil's Vale and copper projects in Chile—our autonomous haul trucks posted record orders. Middle East/Africa grew modestly +3%, led by Saudi Aramco's downstream upgrades, though delays in Nigerian oilfield capex capped upside. Margins here at 20% reflect logistics premiums, but our digital twin simulation services are driving 15% attach rates.

Geographically, we're seeing a 'tri-polarization': North America leading on premium, high-tech demand; APAC scaling volumes in EVs and semis; Europe stabilizing via green tech. FX was a $25 million headwind, but we hedged 80% of exposures. End-market mix shifted +5 points to semis and aero (now 35% of total), versus autos at 30%. Looking ahead, we're guiding FY24 regional growth of 12-15% organic, with North America at 16-18% and APAC at 15-20%. Strategically, our 'Resilient Global Footprint' initiative—$500 million in capex for dual-sourcing and digital factories—positions us like peers Caterpillar and Siemens to capture $50 billion in underserved automation TAM through 2028, per McKinsey estimates. Risks include China stimulus uncertainty and Eurozone inflation, but our 2.5x backlog-to-revenue ratio gives us conviction.

I'd also like to provide a detailed update on one of our key operational metrics: lead times for our core products and components. In the industrial equipment sector, lead times are a critical barometer of supply chain health, customer responsiveness, and our ability to capture market share amid ongoing volatility. We're seeing meaningful progress here, which directly supports our growth outlook and positions us well against peers like Caterpillar, Deere, and Siemens.

Our weighted average lead time across our flagship product lines—including our Precision CNC machining centers, hydraulic forging presses, and modular robotic welding systems—stood at 14.2 weeks at the end of Q2, down from 18.6 weeks prior and a peak of 26 weeks back in Q4 '21 during the height of post-COVID disruptions. That's a 24% quarter-over-quarter improvement and a 45% reduction from our pandemic highs. For context, industry benchmarks from the Association for Manufacturing Technology peg the sector average at around 16-18 weeks for similar capital goods, so we're outperforming by 10-15%.

Drilling down by product category: CNC Machining Centers, 35% of backlog, compressed to 12 weeks from 16 weeks QoQ, driven by stabilized semiconductor availability for our Fanuc-integrated controls. Demand remains robust, with order intake up 12% YoY from automotive OEMs re-shoring production. Hydraulic Forging Presses, 25% of backlog, now at 15 weeks from 20 weeks, thanks to resolved steel slab shortages—these are key for aerospace and heavy truck frames, where we've seen pull-ins from Boeing suppliers amid 737 MAX ramp-ups. Robotic Welding Systems, 20% of backlog, holding steady at 13 weeks, bolstered by our new ABB partnership for collaborative robot arms, benefiting from shorter component lead times, with weld wire and power supplies now at 4-6 weeks versus 10+ earlier this year.

On the components side, critical inputs like high-strength alloy steel castings, sourced primarily from India and domestic foundries, are down to 6.8 weeks from 9.2 weeks, a 26% improvement, reflecting our dual-sourcing strategy post-Ukraine disruptions. Rare earth magnets for servo motors—vital for our electro-hydraulic actuators—have fallen to 8.1 weeks from 12 weeks, as we've shifted 40% of volume away from China to Australian and U.S. miners like Lynas and MP Materials. PLC controllers and HMIs from Rockwell Automation and Schneider Electric are now at 5.2 weeks, aided by the CHIPS Act-fueled U.S. fab expansions.

Regionally: Americas, 55% of revenue, at 11.8 weeks, our strongest, up from our new greenfield facility in Monterrey, Mexico, adding 25% capacity for CNC builds and insulating us from Red Sea shipping delays. EMEA, 25% of revenue, at 14.5 weeks, pressured by energy costs and port strikes but mitigated via Sheffield, UK throughput, with 90% on-time delivery to Airbus and VW. APAC, 20% of revenue, at 18.7 weeks due to tariff frictions and typhoon impacts, but our Suzhou JV with Mitsubishi has cut robotic lead times by 30% YoY.

Driving these trends: demand normalization, with backlog at $2.8 billion, flat QoQ but healthier mix—60% short-cycle. Supply chain resilience via $150 million YTD investments: supplier diversification, onboarding 12 new Tier 1s, reducing single-source dependency to 18%; digital transformation with SAP Ariba AI forecasting at 92% accuracy and digital twins shaving validation cycles; Factory 4.0 upgrades boosting OEE to 88%; inventory optimization with DIO at 72 days. These shorter lead times are a moat—95% on-time delivery drives 15% win rate uplift, 4-6% surcharges adding 200 bps to margins. We expect 12-13 weeks by year-end.

As we wrap up, I'm pleased to provide our outlook for Q3 and full FY2024. We've seen robust end-market demand: semiconductor capex from TSMC/Intel for CNC/wafer systems; EV OEMs ramping battery lines like Tesla/Rivian for robotic welding; aerospace recovery with Boeing/Airbus; reshoring via CHIPS/IRA. Headwinds: steel/electronics inflation, China capex softness, FX.

Q3 Revenue Guidance: $1.35 billion to $1.40 billion, sequential 5-9% growth, 12-16% YoY organic ex-1% FX. By segment: Automation & Robotics (45%), $620M-$650M, +18-22% YoY on Atlas cobots with MindSphere, 30% AI software attach; Fluid Power & Hydraulics (30%), $410M-$430M, +8-12% on wind/electro-hydraulics; Material Handling (25%), $320M flat to +4% on AGVs. By region: North America 55% +15%; EMEA 25% +10%; APAC 15% +5-8%; LatAm 5% +3%. Embeds $50M-$70M from Industry 4.0 digital twins.

Full-Year 2024: $5.25 billion to $5.35 billion, 11-14% total/12-15% organic over $4.72B FY23, surpassing prior guide on 92% book-to-bill. Pricing +3 points. Backlog $4.8B for 9 months visibility. Priorities: supply chain to Mexico/Vietnam (-25% lead times); sustainability/electrification (20% Q3 bookings); $300M M&A; 150bps gross margin to 28.5% via VAVE/ERPNext. Risks: commodities, port strikes; mitigated by $1.2B cash/$1.5B revolver, 50%+ FCF, $400M buybacks.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from Ben Thompson with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Ben Thompson (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the mining and construction markets?

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Good morning, Ben. Thanks for the question. Demand in mining and construction remains resilient, with global mining capex up 12% as noted, driving higher utilization of our haul trucks and excavators. In construction, U.S. non-residential starts are steady, pulling through aftermarket parts like undercarriage components. Our UptimeGuard platform is key here, flagging issues early and boosting service pulls by 35%, which ties directly into the 14.2% aftermarket growth we highlighted.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen (Goldman Sachs):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Michael Rivera (CFO):
Thanks, Lisa. For FY2025, we expect capex in the $500-550 million range, up modestly from this year's $500 million, focused on high-ROI areas like the $150 million Dayton robotics expansion, $200 million Chennai plant for APAC localization, and $120 million dealer densification. This supports lead time compression to 12-13 weeks and margin gains, while maintaining 50%+ FCF conversion.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mark Ruiz with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mark Ruiz (Barclays):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Mark, great question. We've tackled disruptions head-on with $150 million in resilience investments—diversifying suppliers, like shifting rare earths from China and steel from Nucor/JSW, plus SAP Ariba forecasting at 92% accuracy. This drove 24% QoQ lead time improvement and 200 bps gross margin lift from surcharges/on-time delivery. Margins hit 32.1% despite steel inflation, with aftermarket at 48.2% EBITDA providing a buffer. Regional localization, like Monterrey, keeps us agile amid Red Sea or tariff issues.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Apex Industrial Machinery Corp. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
